topic: Provisioning, SCIM and Enterprise Managed Users

notes.front: What is System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM)?
notes.back: An open specification for managing user identities between systems; with Enterprise Managed Users, the IdP uses it to create, manage and deactivate accounts on GitHub.
notes.explanation: To manage members’ accounts on GitHub from the IdP, the IdP must implement SCIM to communicate with GitHub.
notes.example: Like a personnel system that automatically creates, updates and closes staff accounts in every office tool when someone joins, moves or leaves.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Configuring SCIM provisioning for Enterprise Managed Users”
notes.evidence: To create, manage, and deactivate user accounts for your enterprise members on GitHub, your IdP must implement SCIM for communication with GitHub. SCIM is an open specification for management of user identities between systems.

notes.front: For Enterprise Managed Users, what is a partner identity provider?
notes.back: An IdP that GitHub partners with to provide authentication, using SAML or OIDC, and provisioning, using SCIM.
notes.explanation: GitHub offers these as a paved-path integration, and advises using a single partner IdP for both authentication and provisioning.
notes.example: Like a car maker’s approved garage, which services both the engine and the electrics, instead of two unrelated workshops.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Enterprise Managed Users”, “What are partner identity providers?”
notes.evidence: Partner IdPs provide authentication using SAML or OIDC, and provide provisioning with System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM).

notes.front: In an enterprise with managed users, what is the short code?
notes.back: The enterprise’s own short identifier, used in the setup user’s username, SHORTCODE_admin.
notes.explanation: GitHub Docs writes it into usernames such as the setup user’s, replacing SHORTCODE with the enterprise’s own value.
notes.example: Like a company prefix on staff badge numbers, for example a firm whose admin badge reads ACME_admin.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Configuring SCIM provisioning for Enterprise Managed Users”, “Configuring provisioning for other identity management systems”
notes.evidence: replacing SHORTCODE with your enterprise's shortcode.

notes.front: In an enterprise with managed users, what is the setup user?
notes.back: The account used to configure SCIM provisioning for the enterprise.
notes.explanation: It is also the actor recorded in the audit log for group SCIM calls from the IdP.
notes.example: Like the installer’s master login that sets up a building’s access system before any staff badges exist.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing team memberships with identity provider groups”, “About team management with Enterprise Managed Users”
notes.evidence: These events capture detailed information about the call, including the payload and operation performed, and are recorded in the audit log with the actor set to the setup user, the account used to configure SCIM provisioning.

notes.front: What is team synchronization?
notes.back: A feature that synchronizes a GitHub team with an IdP group, so membership changes to the group are reflected on GitHub automatically.
notes.explanation: It reduces the need for manual updates and custom scripts to keep team membership in step with the IdP.
notes.example: Like a mailing list that updates itself from the personnel department’s team lists.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing team synchronization for your organization”, “About team synchronization”
notes.evidence: If team sync is enabled for your organization or enterprise account, you can synchronize a GitHub team with an IdP group. When you do this, membership changes to the IdP group are reflected on GitHub automatically, reducing the need for manual updates and custom scripts.

notes.front: With Enterprise Managed Users, what is an IdP group used for?
notes.back: A group on the identity provider that is connected to a GitHub team, to manage team and organization membership from the IdP.
notes.explanation: GitHub keeps membership in step with the IdP through SCIM provisioning and reconciliation jobs.
notes.example: Like a department list in the company directory that decides who is on a project channel.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing team memberships with identity provider groups”, “About team management with Enterprise Managed Users”
notes.evidence: With Enterprise Managed Users, you can manage team and organization membership within your enterprise through your IdP by connecting teams on GitHub with groups on your IdP.

notes.front: What is the guest collaborator role?
notes.back: An Enterprise Managed Users role for giving limited access to vendors and contractors.
notes.explanation: Guest collaborators are managed user accounts provisioned by the IdP, but their access to internal repositories is narrower than a regular user’s.
notes.example: Like a visitor badge for an outside agency: issued by your own security desk, but opening fewer doors.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Abilities of roles in an enterprise”, “Guest collaborators”
notes.evidence: The guest collaborator role is only available with Enterprise Managed Users. You can use the guest collaborator role to grant limited access to vendors and contractors. Guest collaborators: Are provisioned by your IdP, like all managed user accounts.

notes.front: In an enterprise with managed users, what is a repository collaborator?
notes.back: The name for the outside collaborator role when the enterprise uses managed user accounts.
notes.explanation: Generally, GitHub’s documentation for outside collaborators also applies to repository collaborators.
notes.example: Like calling a contractor a “project associate” in one division: the same job under another name.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “People who consume a license in an organization”, “Organizations on GitHub Enterprise Cloud”
notes.evidence: If your enterprise uses managed user accounts, the outside collaborator role is called "repository collaborator." Generally, the documentation for outside collaborators also applies to repository collaborators.

notes.front: With Enterprise Managed Users, what creates new user accounts on GitHub, and where must users authenticate?
notes.back: The IdP provisions the accounts, with access to the enterprise, and users must authenticate on the IdP.
notes.explanation: Lifecycle and authentication are both run from the external identity management system rather than by users.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Enterprise Managed Users”, “What are Enterprise Managed Users in GitHub?”
notes.evidence: Your IdP provisions new user accounts on GitHub, with access to your enterprise. Users must authenticate on your IdP to access your enterprise's resources on GitHub.

notes.front: With Enterprise Managed Users, which account details does the company control from its IdP?
notes.back: Usernames, profile data, organization membership and repository access.
notes.explanation: Because these details come from the IdP, a managed user cannot change their profile name or email address on GitHub; the change has to be made in the IdP.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Enterprise Managed Users”, “What are Enterprise Managed Users in GitHub?”
notes.evidence: You control usernames, profile data, organization membership, and repository access from your IdP.

notes.front: In an enterprise with managed users, a developer wants to change their display name. Where does the change have to be made?
notes.back: C) In the company’s IdP
notes.explanation: Profile data is controlled from the IdP, and managed users cannot change their profile name on GitHub.
notes.choices:
A) In the developer’s GitHub profile settings
B) In the organization’s settings
C) In the company’s IdP
D) By opening a GitHub Support ticket
notes.choicesExplained: A) Managed user accounts cannot change their profile name on GitHub. B) Organization settings do not hold members’ profile data. D) GitHub Support is not the source of profile data; the IdP is.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Enterprise Managed Users”, “What are Enterprise Managed Users in GitHub?”
notes.evidence: You control usernames, profile data, organization membership, and repository access from your IdP.

notes.front: How does GitHub create a managed user’s username, and what can cause a conflict?
notes.back: By normalising an identifier the IdP provides; a conflict may occur if normalisation removes the identifier’s unique parts.
notes.explanation: Two identifiers that differ only in the parts normalisation strips out would become the same username.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Enterprise Managed Users”, “How are usernames and profile information managed for EMUs?”
notes.evidence: GitHub automatically creates a username for each developer by normalizing an identifier provided by your IdP. If the unique parts of the identifier are removed during normalization, a conflict may occur.

notes.front: Where do a managed user account’s profile name and email address come from, and how many email addresses can there be?
notes.back: From the IdP, which can provide only one email address; the user cannot change either on GitHub.
notes.explanation: Since the IdP is the source, edits have to be made there rather than on GitHub.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Enterprise Managed Users”, “How are usernames and profile information managed for EMUs?”
notes.evidence: The profile name and email address of a managed user account is provided by the IdP: Managed user accounts cannot change their profile name or email address on GitHub. The IdP can only provide one email address.

notes.front: When assigning users to the GitHub application in the IdP, how do you set each user’s role in the enterprise?
notes.back: With the “Roles” attribute in the IdP application.
notes.explanation: Roles such as member, owner or guest collaborator are therefore given from the IdP, like the rest of the account.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Configuring SCIM provisioning for Enterprise Managed Users”, “Assigning users and groups”
notes.evidence: When assigning users, you can use the "Roles" attribute in the application on your IdP to set a user's role in your enterprise.

notes.front: Which three partner IdPs does GitHub list for Enterprise Managed Users?
notes.back: Microsoft Entra ID, Okta and PingFederate.
notes.explanation: Each has an application that handles both authentication and provisioning, which simplifies SCIM configuration.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Configuring SCIM provisioning for Enterprise Managed Users”, “Configuring provisioning if you use a partner IdP’s application”
notes.evidence: If you use a partner IdP, you can simplify the configuration of SCIM provisioning by using the partner IdP's application.

notes.front: When you use a single partner IdP for both authentication and provisioning, what does GitHub support?
notes.back: The application on the partner IdP and the IdP’s integration with GitHub.
notes.explanation: That full support is why GitHub advises one partner IdP for both jobs.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Enterprise Managed Users”, “What are partner identity providers?”
notes.evidence: When you use a single partner IdP for both authentication and provisioning, GitHub provides support for the application on the partner IdP and the IdP's integration with GitHub.

notes.front: A company already uses Okta and wants the setup for Enterprise Managed Users that GitHub fully supports. What should it do?
notes.back: B) Use Okta for both authentication and provisioning
notes.explanation: Okta is a partner IdP, and using one partner IdP for both jobs is the route GitHub supports fully.
notes.choices:
A) Use Okta for authentication and another system for provisioning
B) Use Okta for both authentication and provisioning
C) Use Okta only for team synchronization
D) Build its own provisioning scripts against GitHub’s SCIM endpoints
notes.choicesExplained: A) Mixing systems is not expressly supported. C) Team synchronization is not how accounts are provisioned for Enterprise Managed Users. D) Custom provisioning is for systems that are not partner IdPs, and support may be limited.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Enterprise Managed Users”, “What are partner identity providers?”
notes.evidence: When you use a single partner IdP for both authentication and provisioning, GitHub provides support for the application on the partner IdP and the IdP's integration with GitHub.

notes.front: If you cannot use a single partner IdP for both jobs, what must another identity management system provide?
notes.back: Authentication using SAML 2.0 and user lifecycle management using SCIM 2.0, following GitHub’s integration guidelines.
notes.explanation: GitHub does not test every such system, and its support team may not be able to help with mixed or untested ones.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Enterprise Managed Users”, “Can I use identity management systems other than the supported partners?”
notes.evidence: adhering to SAML 2.0 specification Provide user lifecycle management using SCIM

notes.front: Is it supported to use Okta for SSO and Entra ID for SCIM, or the other way round?
notes.back: No. The combination of Okta and Entra ID for SSO and SCIM, in either order, is explicitly not supported.
notes.explanation: Either order counts, so Okta for sign-in with Entra ID for provisioning is ruled out as much as the reverse.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Enterprise Managed Users”, “Can I use identity management systems other than the supported partners?”
notes.evidence: The combination of Okta and Entra ID for SSO and SCIM (in either order) is explicitly not supported

notes.front: A company plans Okta for SAML sign-in and Entra ID for SCIM provisioning in its enterprise with managed users. What will happen when Entra ID tries to provision users?
notes.back: B) GitHub’s SCIM endpoint returns an error, because this combination is not supported
notes.explanation: GitHub explicitly rejects Okta with Entra ID for SSO and SCIM, and returns an error on provisioning attempts.
notes.choices:
A) It works, with limited support
B) GitHub’s SCIM endpoint returns an error, because this combination is not supported
C) It works only for guest collaborators
D) It works once team synchronization is enabled
notes.choicesExplained: A) Limited support is for untested systems, not this combination, which is explicitly unsupported. D) Team synchronization does not change provisioning. C) Guest collaborators are provisioned the same way as everyone else.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Configuring SCIM provisioning for Enterprise Managed Users”, “Configuring provisioning for other identity management systems”
notes.evidence: GitHub's SCIM API will return an error to the identity provider on provisioning attempts if this combination is configured.

notes.front: Can managed user accounts create public content or collaborate outside the enterprise?
notes.back: No, neither.
notes.explanation: The accounts belong to the enterprise and are confined to its resources.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About Enterprise Managed Users”, “What are Enterprise Managed Users in GitHub?”
notes.evidence: Managed user accounts cannot create public content or collaborate outside your enterprise.

notes.front: On GitHub.com, what can managed user accounts do with public repositories outside the enterprise?
notes.back: View them, but not interact: no pushing, issues, pull requests, discussions, comments, reactions, stars, watching or forking.
notes.explanation: They have read-only access to the wider GitHub community.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Abilities and restrictions of managed user accounts”, “Interactions”
notes.evidence: On GitHub.com, managed user accounts can view all public repositories, but cannot interact with repositories outside of the enterprise in any of the following ways: Push code to the repository Create issues or pull requests within the repository

notes.front: Who can see managed user accounts and the content they create?
notes.back: Only other members of the enterprise.
notes.explanation: Other GitHub users cannot see, mention or invite them to collaborate.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Abilities and restrictions of managed user accounts”, “Visibility and invitations”
notes.evidence: Are only visible, along with the content they create, to other members of the enterprise. Cannot be seen, mentioned, or invited to collaborate by other GitHub users.

notes.front: Can managed user accounts be invited to organizations or repositories outside the enterprise?
notes.back: No, nor to other enterprises.
notes.explanation: Their collaboration stays inside the enterprise that owns them.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Abilities and restrictions of managed user accounts”, “Visibility and invitations”
notes.evidence: Cannot be invited to organizations or repositories outside of the enterprise, or to other enterprises.

notes.front: A managed user wants to open an issue on a popular open-source library on GitHub.com to report a bug. What can they do with their managed user account?
notes.back: B) Only view the repository; they cannot open issues outside the enterprise
notes.explanation: Managed user accounts can view public repositories but cannot create issues, fork or star outside the enterprise.
notes.choices:
A) Open the issue, since the repository is public
B) Only view the repository; they cannot open issues outside the enterprise
C) Star the repository to follow it
D) Fork the repository and open a pull request instead
notes.choicesExplained: A) Public visibility does not allow interaction for managed users. D) Forking outside repositories is also blocked. C) Starring is blocked too.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Abilities and restrictions of managed user accounts”, “Interactions”
notes.evidence: On GitHub.com, managed user accounts can view all public repositories, but cannot interact with repositories outside of the enterprise in any of the following ways:

notes.front: Which repository visibilities can be created in organizations owned by an enterprise with managed users?
notes.back: Only private and internal, depending on organization and enterprise repository visibility settings.
notes.explanation: Public repositories are ruled out because managed users cannot create public content.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Abilities and restrictions of managed user accounts”, “Repository management”
notes.evidence: Only private and internal repositories can be created in organizations owned by an enterprise with managed users, depending on organization and enterprise repository visibility settings.

notes.front: If an enterprise allows managed users to own repositories, what can those repositories be, and whom can they invite?
notes.back: Only private repositories, and they can invite only other enterprise members to collaborate.
notes.explanation: Whether managed users can create user-owned repositories at all is the enterprise’s choice.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Abilities and restrictions of managed user accounts”, “Repository management”
notes.evidence: If you allow managed user accounts to create repositories owned by their user accounts, they can only own private repositories and can only invite other enterprise members to collaborate on their user-owned repositories.

notes.front: A team in an enterprise with managed users wants to publish an open-source library from one of the enterprise’s organizations as a public repository. What happens?
notes.back: A) They cannot: only private and internal repositories can be created there
notes.explanation: Organizations owned by an enterprise with managed users allow only private and internal repositories.
notes.choices:
A) They cannot: only private and internal repositories can be created there
B) They can, if an organization owner approves
C) They can, as a user-owned public repository
D) They can, once team synchronization is on
notes.choicesExplained: B) No approval unlocks public repositories in these organizations. C) User-owned repositories of managed users can only be private. D) Team synchronization has nothing to do with visibility.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Abilities and restrictions of managed user accounts”, “Repository management”
notes.evidence: Only private and internal repositories can be created in organizations owned by an enterprise with managed users

notes.front: Can GitHub-hosted runners be used for repositories owned by managed user accounts?
notes.back: No. They can be used in repositories owned by organizations, but not in repositories owned by managed user accounts.
notes.explanation: Managed user accounts also cannot create workflow templates for GitHub Actions.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Abilities and restrictions of managed user accounts”, “GitHub Actions”
notes.evidence: Managed user accounts cannot create workflow templates for GitHub Actions. While GitHub-hosted runners can be used in repositories owned by organizations, they are not available for repositories owned by managed user accounts.

notes.front: When can a managed user account install a GitHub App on a repository?
notes.back: When the app does not request organization permissions and the user has admin access to the repository.
notes.explanation: Installing on a whole organization instead needs the user to be an organization owner.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Abilities and restrictions of managed user accounts”, “GitHub Apps”
notes.evidence: Can install GitHub Apps on a repository if the app doesn't request organization permissions and if the managed user account has admin access to the repository. Can install GitHub Apps on an organization if the managed user account is an organization owner.

notes.front: With SCIM, what does the IdP do when you assign a group to the GitHub application?
notes.back: It provisions accounts for all members of the group.
notes.explanation: Provisioned accounts are added to the enterprise as they are created.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Configuring SCIM provisioning for Enterprise Managed Users”, “About user lifecycle management with SCIM”
notes.evidence: After you configure provisioning for Enterprise Managed Users, your IdP uses SCIM to provision user accounts on GitHub and add the accounts to your enterprise. If you assign a group to the application in your IdP, your IdP will provision accounts for all members of the group.

notes.front: With SCIM, what happens on GitHub when you update information about a user’s identity on the IdP?
notes.back: The IdP updates the user’s account on GitHub.
notes.explanation: The IdP stays the source of truth, and SCIM carries its changes across.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Configuring SCIM provisioning for Enterprise Managed Users”, “About user lifecycle management with SCIM”
notes.evidence: When you update information associated with a user's identity on your IdP, your IdP will update the user's account on GitHub.

notes.front: With SCIM, what happens when you unassign a user from the IdP application or deactivate them on the IdP?
notes.back: Sessions are invalidated and the account disabled; its information is kept, and the username becomes a hash, with the short code appended if applicable.
notes.explanation: Reassigning or reactivating the user later reactivates the account and restores the username.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Configuring SCIM provisioning for Enterprise Managed Users”, “About user lifecycle management with SCIM”
notes.evidence: When you unassign the user from the IdP application or deactivate a user's account on your IdP, your IdP will communicate with GitHub to invalidate any sessions and disable the member's account. The disabled account's information is maintained and their username is changed to a hash of their original username, with the short code appended if applicable.

notes.front: With SCIM, what happens when a deprovisioned user is reassigned to the IdP application or reactivated?
notes.back: The account is reactivated and the original username is restored.
notes.explanation: This reverses deprovisioning, which disabled the account and replaced its username with a hash.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Configuring SCIM provisioning for Enterprise Managed Users”, “About user lifecycle management with SCIM”
notes.evidence: If you reassign a user to the IdP application or reactivate their account on your IdP, the user account will be reactivated, and the username will be restored.

notes.front: An engineer leaves and is deactivated in the IdP; six months later they rejoin and are reactivated there. What do they find on GitHub?
notes.back: A) Their old account reactivated, with its original username restored
notes.explanation: Deprovisioning disables the account and hashes the username; reactivating on the IdP reverses both.
notes.choices:
A) Their old account reactivated, with its original username restored
B) A brand-new account with a new username
C) Their old account, still disabled until GitHub Support restores it
D) Their old account, still under the hashed username
notes.choicesExplained: B) The old account’s information was kept, so no new account is needed. C) Reactivation on the IdP is enough; no support ticket is needed. D) The hash is replaced when the username is restored.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Configuring SCIM provisioning for Enterprise Managed Users”, “About user lifecycle management with SCIM”
notes.evidence: If you reassign a user to the IdP application or reactivate their account on your IdP, the user account will be reactivated, and the username will be restored.

notes.front: If you do not use a partner IdP for provisioning, how can you manage user lifecycles, and with which enterprises is that not supported?
notes.back: By calling GitHub’s own SCIM provisioning endpoints directly; this is not supported for enterprises enabled for OIDC.
notes.explanation: The setup user turns it on with the “Enable open SCIM configuration” option.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Configuring SCIM provisioning for Enterprise Managed Users”, “Configuring provisioning for other identity management systems”
notes.evidence: If you don't use a partner IdP, or if you only use a partner IdP for SAML authentication, you can manage the lifecycle of user accounts using GitHub's REST API endpoints for SCIM provisioning.

notes.front: Can you configure SCIM for an enterprise account that was not created for Enterprise Managed Users?
notes.back: No. Without Enterprise Managed Users, SCIM provisioning needs SAML SSO configured at organization level, not enterprise level.
notes.explanation: Enterprise-level SCIM exists only for enterprises with managed users.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About SAML for enterprise IAM”, “About SAML SSO for your enterprise”
notes.evidence: You cannot configure SCIM for your enterprise account unless your account was created for Enterprise Managed Users. For more information, see About Enterprise Managed Users. If you do not use Enterprise Managed Users, and you want to use SCIM provisioning, you must configure SAML SSO at the organization level, not the enterprise level.

notes.front: An enterprise with personal accounts uses enterprise-level SAML SSO and now wants SCIM provisioning. What does GitHub Docs say it must do?
notes.back: A) Configure SAML SSO at organization level instead, and use SCIM there
notes.explanation: Without Enterprise Managed Users, SCIM is only available with organization-level SAML SSO.
notes.choices:
A) Configure SAML SSO at organization level instead, and use SCIM there
B) Enable SCIM on the enterprise account
C) Turn on team synchronization, which provisions users
D) Nothing: SCIM is on by default
notes.choicesExplained: B) Enterprise-level SCIM needs an enterprise created for Enterprise Managed Users. C) Team synchronization is not a provisioning service. D) SCIM is not on by default.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About SAML for enterprise IAM”, “About SAML SSO for your enterprise”
notes.evidence: If you do not use Enterprise Managed Users, and you want to use SCIM provisioning, you must configure SAML SSO at the organization level, not the enterprise level.

notes.front: How do you reset the setup user’s password?
notes.back: Contact GitHub Support through the Support portal; the usual email-based reset does not work.
notes.explanation: The setup user is a special account, so the normal password reset option is not available for it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Configuring SCIM provisioning for Enterprise Managed Users”, “Configuring provisioning for other identity management systems”
notes.evidence: If you need to reset the password for your setup user, contact GitHub Support through the GitHub Support portal. The usual password reset option by providing your email address will not work.

notes.front: Which IdP and SAML set-up do you need to enable team synchronization for an enterprise account?
notes.back: Microsoft Entra ID as the IdP, with SAML configured at the enterprise level.
notes.explanation: Enterprise-level team sync then lets organization owners and team maintainers sync teams in all the enterprise’s organizations.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing team synchronization for organizations in your enterprise”, “About team synchronization for enterprise accounts”
notes.evidence: If you use SAML at the enterprise level with Entra ID as your IdP, you can enable team synchronization for your enterprise account to allow organization owners and team maintainers to synchronize teams in the organizations owned by your enterprise accounts with IdP groups.

notes.front: Which IdPs can you use for team synchronization in an organization?
notes.back: Entra ID commercial tenants (not Gov Cloud) and Okta.
notes.explanation: Okta appears only at organization level; enterprise-level team sync is for Entra ID.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing team synchronization for your organization”, “About team synchronization”
notes.evidence: You can use team synchronization with supported IdPs. Entra ID commercial tenants (Gov Cloud is not supported) Okta

notes.front: An enterprise with personal accounts uses Okta for enterprise-level SAML and wants team synchronization across all its organizations. What is the obstacle?
notes.back: C) Team sync for enterprise-level SAML is only available with Microsoft Entra ID
notes.explanation: Okta team synchronization is available only for individual organizations, and enterprise-level team sync needs Entra ID.
notes.choices:
A) Okta does not support SAML
B) Team synchronization needs Enterprise Managed Users
C) Team sync for enterprise-level SAML is only available with Microsoft Entra ID
D) There is none: it works with any IdP
notes.choicesExplained: A) Okta is an officially supported SAML IdP. B) Team synchronization serves enterprises without managed users; an enterprise with managed users does not need it. D) Enterprise-level team sync is tied to Entra ID.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Deciding whether to configure SAML for your enterprise or your organizations”
notes.evidence: SCIM is not available for enterprise accounts without Enterprise Managed Users, and team synchronization is only available for SAML at the enterprise level if you use Microsoft Entra ID (previously known as Azure AD) as an IdP.

notes.front: Does team synchronization add people who are not yet organization members?
notes.back: Not in most cases. It is not a user provisioning service; a user is added to a team only if already an organization member.
notes.explanation: You can optionally let it re-invite people who were previously members and have since been removed.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing team synchronization for organizations in your enterprise”, “About team synchronization for enterprise accounts”
notes.evidence: Team synchronization is not a user provisioning service and does not invite non-members to join organizations in most cases. This means a user will only be successfully added to a team if they are already an organization member. However, you can optionally allow team synchronization to re-invite users who were previously organization members and have since been removed.

notes.front: A team is synced with an Entra ID group. A new hire, never an organization member, is added to the group but does not appear in the team. Why?
notes.back: B) Team synchronization is not a provisioning service and adds only existing organization members
notes.explanation: The new hire must first become an organization member; team sync does not invite non-members in most cases.
notes.choices:
A) The group must be a Microsoft 365 group
B) Team synchronization is not a provisioning service and adds only existing organization members
C) Team sync runs only once a week
D) The team has passed its member limit
notes.choicesExplained: A) Nothing points to the group type, and someone who is not an organization member is not added whatever the group. C) GitHub Docs gives no weekly schedule. D) One new hire is far below the 5,000-member team limit.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing team synchronization for organizations in your enterprise”, “About team synchronization for enterprise accounts”
notes.evidence: This means a user will only be successfully added to a team if they are already an organization member.

notes.front: For team synchronization, what are the member limits for a GitHub team and for an organization?
notes.back: 5,000 members per team and 10,000 members per organization.
notes.explanation: Going over them degrades performance and may cause synchronization failures.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing team synchronization for organizations in your enterprise”, “Usage limits”
notes.evidence: Exceeding these limits will lead to a degradation in performance and may cause synchronization failures. Maximum number of members in a GitHub team: 5,000 Maximum number of members in a GitHub organization: 10,000

notes.front: For team synchronization, what is the maximum number of teams in an organization, and does the limit apply to SCIM-based linking?
notes.back: 1,500 teams; the limits do not apply to SCIM-based linking of teams to SCIM groups.
notes.explanation: An organization may have more teams than this, but its use of team synchronization will be impaired.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing team synchronization for organizations in your enterprise”, “Usage limits”
notes.evidence: Maximum number of teams in a GitHub organization: 1,500 These limits only apply to the use of the team synchronization feature. Your organization may have more members or teams than the limits above, but your use of the team synchronization feature will be impaired. These limits do not apply to SCIM-based linking of teams to SCIM groups.

notes.front: When you disable team synchronization, what happens to members who were added to a team through the IdP group?
notes.back: They are not removed from the team and keep their access to repositories.
notes.explanation: Disabling does not undo membership already given through the IdP group.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing team synchronization for organizations in your enterprise”, “About team synchronization for enterprise accounts”
notes.evidence: When you disable team synchronization, any team members that were assigned to a GitHub team through the IdP group are not removed from the team and retain their access to repositories.

notes.front: Does an enterprise with managed users need team synchronization?
notes.back: No. It can manage team membership through the SCIM configuration created when setting up the enterprise.
notes.explanation: IdP groups connected through SCIM do the job that team sync does for other enterprises.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing team synchronization for organizations in your enterprise”
notes.evidence: If your enterprise uses Enterprise Managed Users, you do not need to use team synchronization. Instead, you can manage team membership via the SCIM configuration you created while setting up your enterprise.

notes.front: What is the key difference between SCIM provisioning and team synchronization?
notes.back: SCIM creates, updates and deactivates user accounts; team synchronization only syncs team membership for people who are already organization members.
notes.explanation: GitHub Docs stresses that team synchronization is not a user provisioning service.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing team synchronization for organizations in your enterprise”, “About team synchronization for enterprise accounts”
notes.evidence: Team synchronization is not a user provisioning service and does not invite non-members to join organizations in most cases. This means a user will only be successfully added to a team if they are already an organization member.

notes.front: A company wants leavers’ GitHub accounts to be disabled automatically when the personnel team deactivates them in the IdP. Which mechanism does that?
notes.back: D) SCIM provisioning
notes.explanation: SCIM is how the IdP disables an account on GitHub; team synchronization does not provision users.
notes.choices:
A) Team synchronization
B) An SSH certificate authority
C) Organization-level 2FA requirement
D) SCIM provisioning
notes.choicesExplained: A) Team synchronization syncs team membership and is not a provisioning service. B) An SSH CA governs Git access over SSH. C) Requiring 2FA does not react to IdP changes.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing team synchronization for organizations in your enterprise”, “About team synchronization for enterprise accounts”
notes.evidence: Team synchronization is not a user provisioning service

notes.front: If an IdP group change adds a user to a team in an organization they are not yet a member of, what does GitHub do?
notes.back: It automatically adds the user to the organization.
notes.explanation: Unlike team synchronization, IdP groups with Enterprise Managed Users can bring people into organizations.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing team memberships with identity provider groups”, “About team management with Enterprise Managed Users”
notes.evidence: When a change to an IdP group or a new team connection results in a user joining a team in an organization they were not already a member of, GitHub automatically adds the user to the organization.

notes.front: When you disconnect an IdP group from a team, whom does GitHub remove from the organization?
notes.back: Users who became organization members through that team membership and have no other route into the organization.
notes.explanation: Members who belong to the organization by other means keep their membership.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing team memberships with identity provider groups”, “About team management with Enterprise Managed Users”
notes.evidence: When you disconnect a group from a team, GitHub removes users who became members of the organization via team membership if they do not have membership in the organization by any other means.

notes.front: Before you can connect an IdP group with a team on GitHub, what must you do in the IdP?
notes.back: Assign the group to the GitHub Enterprise Managed User application.
notes.explanation: GitHub Docs lists this as a requirement for connecting IdP groups with teams.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing team memberships with identity provider groups”, “Requirements for connecting IdP groups with teams”
notes.evidence: Before you can connect an IdP group with a team on GitHub, you must assign the group to the GitHub Enterprise Managed User application in your IdP.

notes.front: How many IdP groups can one team be connected to, and can one group serve several teams?
notes.back: One group per team; the same IdP group can be assigned to multiple teams.
notes.explanation: The limit is on the team side only, so a group can feed several teams.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing team memberships with identity provider groups”, “Requirements for connecting IdP groups with teams”
notes.evidence: You can connect a team in your enterprise to one IdP group. You can assign the same IdP group to multiple teams in your enterprise.

notes.front: How often does GitHub reconcile team membership with stored IdP group data?
notes.back: Daily, and also whenever a group SCIM call updates membership or an admin links or unlinks a team.
notes.explanation: Reconciliation keeps team membership on GitHub in step with the group data sent from the IdP.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing team memberships with identity provider groups”, “About team management with Enterprise Managed Users”
notes.evidence: Once GitHub stores the group data at the enterprise level, it runs a daily reconciliation job to synchronize team membership with the stored IdP group data. This reconciliation also runs whenever a Group SCIM API call updates group membership, and if an admin links or unlinks a team to a stored group.

notes.front: Can a team connected to an IdP group be a parent or child team?
notes.back: No. It can be neither the parent of other teams nor the child of another team.
notes.explanation: For a nested team, GitHub recommends creating a new team or removing the nested relationships first.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing team memberships with identity provider groups”, “About team management with Enterprise Managed Users”
notes.evidence: Teams connected to IdP groups cannot be parents of other teams nor a child of another team. If the team you want to connect to an IdP group is a parent or child team, we recommend creating a new team or removing the nested relationships that make your team a parent team.

notes.front: If a team’s membership is managed with an IdP group, can you give one of its members the team maintainer role?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: Membership comes from the IdP, and the team maintainer role cannot be assigned in such a team.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing team memberships with identity provider groups”, “About team management with Enterprise Managed Users”
notes.evidence: If you are managing a team's membership with an IdP group, you cannot assign the team maintainer role to a member of that team.

notes.front: Where do you manage repository access for a team connected to an IdP group?
notes.back: On GitHub, as for any team in the enterprise.
notes.explanation: The IdP group decides who is in the team; what the team can reach is still set on GitHub.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing team memberships with identity provider groups”, “About team management with Enterprise Managed Users”
notes.evidence: To manage repository access for any team in your enterprise, including teams connected to an IdP group, you must make changes on GitHub.

notes.front: Connecting an existing team to an IdP group: what must happen first, and where are membership changes made afterwards?
notes.back: Remove manually added members first; afterwards the IdP administrator makes membership changes in the IdP, not on GitHub.
notes.explanation: Once connected, team membership can no longer be managed directly on GitHub.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing team memberships with identity provider groups”, “Requirements for connecting IdP groups with teams”
notes.evidence: If you are connecting an existing team to an IdP group, you must first remove any members that were added manually. After you connect a team in your enterprise to an IdP group, your IdP administrator must make team membership changes through the identity provider. You cannot manage team membership directly on GitHub.

notes.front: A team is connected to an IdP group. Its lead wants to add one more person and give the team write access to a new repository. Where is each change made?
notes.back: B) The person is added in the IdP group; repository access is set on GitHub
notes.explanation: Membership comes only from the IdP, while repository access for every team is changed on GitHub.
notes.choices:
A) Both on GitHub
B) The person is added in the IdP group; repository access is set on GitHub
C) Both in the IdP
D) The person is added on GitHub; repository access is set in the IdP
notes.choicesExplained: A) Membership of an IdP-connected team cannot be managed on GitHub. C) Repository access is not set in the IdP. D) This reverses the two.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing team memberships with identity provider groups”, “About team management with Enterprise Managed Users”
notes.evidence: To manage repository access for any team in your enterprise, including teams connected to an IdP group, you must make changes on GitHub.

notes.front: With Microsoft Entra ID as the IdP, which kind of group can be connected to a team?
notes.back: Only a security group; nested group memberships and Microsoft 365 groups are not supported.
notes.explanation: Choosing another group type in Entra ID means the connection cannot be made.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Managing team memberships with identity provider groups”, “Requirements for connecting IdP groups with teams”
notes.evidence: If you use Microsoft Entra ID (previously known as Azure AD) as your IdP, you can only connect a team to a security group. Nested group memberships and Microsoft 365 groups are not supported.

notes.front: Which internal repositories can a guest collaborator access?
notes.back: None, except in organizations where they are added as a member.
notes.explanation: Guest collaborators can be added as organization members or as collaborators in repositories.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Abilities of roles in an enterprise”, “Guest collaborators”
notes.evidence: Can be added as organization members or as collaborators in repositories. Cannot access internal repositories in the enterprise, except in organizations where they're added as a member.

notes.front: What is the difference between a guest collaborator and a regular user when each joins one organization?
notes.back: A regular user automatically gets access to all internal repositories in the enterprise; a guest collaborator does not.
notes.explanation: GitHub Docs offers the guest role for granting limited access to vendors and contractors.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Abilities of roles in an enterprise”, “Guest collaborators”
notes.evidence: The difference between a guest collaborator and a regular user is that when a regular user is added to one organization, they can automatically access all internal repositories in the enterprise.

notes.front: An enterprise with managed users hires a contractor who must work in one organization but must not see internal repositories in the enterprise’s other organizations. Which role fits?
notes.back: D) Guest collaborator
notes.explanation: A guest collaborator reaches internal repositories only in organizations where they are a member.
notes.choices:
A) Enterprise owner
B) A regular member
C) Repository collaborator in every organization
D) Guest collaborator
notes.choicesExplained: A) An owner has wide access, the opposite of what is needed. B) A regular member of one organization can reach all internal repositories in the enterprise. C) Adding them everywhere widens access instead of limiting it.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Abilities of roles in an enterprise”, “Guest collaborators”
notes.evidence: You can use the guest collaborator role to grant limited access to vendors and contractors.

notes.front: What does adding a managed user account to an organization-owned repository as a repository collaborator give them?
notes.back: Access to repositories in organizations where they are not members.
notes.explanation: It is the managed-users version of an outside collaborator, giving access repository by repository.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Abilities and restrictions of managed user accounts”, “Visibility and invitations”
notes.evidence: Can be added to organization-owned repositories as repository collaborators, giving them access to repositories in organizations where they are not members
